scenes.title: Managing Data for Generative AI
scenes.narration: Welcome to Module Two. In the opening diagram, start at the far left with raw data sources: documents, database tables, images, and audio. They do not all arrive in the same structure, and that makes them difficult to use directly in an AI application. Follow the orange arrow into the preparation stage. We extract relevant content, transform it into usable formats, and structure it so the next services can process it consistently. The third box separates a content store from model request data. A content store keeps organized, searchable information, while the model request uses a defined input structure such as JSON. Finally, on the far right, a generative AI application uses those prepared inputs to provide an answer or complete a task. The orange takeaway at the bottom summarizes the architecture: better structure leads to better model inputs. The model's reasoning ability cannot compensate for a corrupted document, missing field, or badly prepared retrieval result. Throughout this module we will study the services and techniques that connect raw enterprise data to reliable AI workflows.

scenes.title: Structured Data: Start with the Shape
scenes.narration: Here we start with structured data. Look at the table on the left. Each row has predictable columns such as customer identifier, issue type, priority, and date. Underneath is the JSON representation of a similar record. These two formats are different to read, but both describe a known schema. Follow the arrow into validation. We check whether the fields match the expected schema, whether types are correct, and whether required values are present. That middle stage prevents malformed records from reaching the application. On the right is the consuming system, which can read and display records consistently because both sides agree on their shape. Now read the orange box along the bottom: the schema is part of the contract. For example, if a downstream system expects priority to be a known category, allowing arbitrary values can break routing or evaluation. In a generative AI application, this matters when tools, databases, or model-generated JSON must communicate predictably. Good prompting is helpful, but applications still need actual validation.

scenes.title: Bedrock Requests Are JSON
scenes.narration: Amazon Bedrock receives model requests through a supported API schema, and this slide makes that contract visible. The application on the left constructs a JSON request. Notice the important fields in the example: a model identifier selects the target model, system and message structures provide the conversation, and inference configuration controls supported generation settings. Follow the arrow from the request payload into Bedrock on the right. The Bedrock runtime interprets the request according to the chosen operation and model's supported features. The three boxes at the bottom explain what is and is not universal. The application supplies a valid request shape. JSON is the transport structure. But the model's native fields, message schema, and supported parameters can differ by API and foundation model. In this example, think of the message asking for a simple explanation of a container. The developer should not copy arbitrary request keys from one model to another and assume they all work. Instead, use the correct model-specific invocation format or the consistent Converse API where supported, then validate responses before passing them downstream.

scenes.title: SageMaker Endpoint Input and Output
scenes.narration: Now compare Bedrock with a SageMaker AI endpoint. Follow the five boxes across the top. A client submits a request, the application serializes the input into a known format, the SageMaker endpoint performs inference, and a deserialization layer interprets the response before the application uses it. Look at the two format examples below. A language model might receive JSON with a prompt and return JSON containing generated text. A classical machine-learning model could receive CSV feature values and return a prediction in CSV or another supported format. Neither format is chosen automatically just because the endpoint is called. The developer and the deployed inference container must agree on content type, payload schema, and response format. The orange warning at the bottom is important: SageMaker endpoints do not magically restructure arbitrary data for an application. You must serialize the request in the expected format, set the required headers, and parse the response correctly. This is a common distinction in AWS design questions about model endpoints and application integration.

scenes.title: Unstructured Text Loses Structure
scenes.narration: Here is a classic problem with unstructured text. On the left is an employee benefits document that has been flattened into one long block of text. In that block, section headings, document metadata, and relationships between benefits and eligibility can be difficult to distinguish. The right side preserves the document structure. Notice the title, employee-benefit table, retirement-plan section, and section links. Those elements provide useful context for answering employee questions. Along the bottom, the transformation pattern tells us to convert source documents into a representation that retains sections, tables, headings, and metadata whenever possible. Better retrieval follows because relevant passages can be found and cited precisely. A model might produce a fluent answer from badly flattened text, but that doesn't guarantee it associates the right rule with the right section. When preparing documents for RAG, preserving meaning and provenance matters just as much as extracting all the characters.

scenes.title: Divider Strings for Better Chunking
scenes.narration: This slide shows one practical technique for turning document structure into retrieval units. On the left is an HTML page about serverless architecture. Its heading tags, such as h1 and h2, identify major sections, but a naïve text extraction process might remove those boundaries. The middle panel shows an ingestion preprocessor converting the HTML heading tags into explicit section-break markers. Read the transformed extract: introduction, how it works, and use cases remain separate, meaningful sections. On the right, the chunking stage uses those markers to produce coherent chunks rather than cutting straight through unrelated topics. The important distinction is that divider strings are part of our preprocessing strategy, not a universal magic keyword recognized by every vector store. Different loaders and splitters can be configured differently. We choose separators that reflect the real document hierarchy so each retrieved chunk contains enough context to support an accurate answer without unnecessary unrelated text.

scenes.title: Format a Conversation for Converse API
scenes.narration: Conversation data also needs a predictable structure. The slide starts with three messages on the left: the user asks a question, the assistant answers, and the user asks a follow-up. Notice the different role labels and colors. In the JSON representation on the right, those messages become entries in the messages array, with a role and content blocks for each entry. The order matters because the model needs to understand which statement came first and which speaker provided it. In this example, the first user asks about a container, the assistant explains it, and the next user requests a real-world example. The system should preserve that interaction rather than treating the follow-up as an unrelated question. The Bedrock Converse API supports a consistent messages-oriented request structure for compatible models, though individual content blocks and capabilities still vary. When writing application code, validate the message roles and content types, enforce context limits, and protect any sensitive data carried in the history. That brings us from raw documents to well-structured model requests. Next we'll examine Bedrock Data Automation for extracting structure from multiple kinds of content.
